title: Where do I even start?
spec: M12 · the layered CLAUDE.md, and what it actually cost
intro: Split the root instruction file into a root file plus per-module files, watch what the agent does differently — then read our own measurement of the pattern, which is a +2% wash on a 9,195-file repo and a −10% win on a 36-file one. The pattern is real. The free lunch is not.

provenance.source: the orderflow setup is narrated over labs/sample-project; steps 4 and 5 carry the course's own measured grids, cited per step

foot: Run it for real: M12's Hands-On builds the pair on labs/sample-project/; the measurement lives in labs/CAPSTONE-2-java-token-benchmark/live_bench/.

steps.title: One file, 340 lines, loaded every session
narrative: orderflow's instructions started the way most repos' do: one root CLAUDE.md that grew every time somebody got burned. Commit format, FastAPI conventions, the event-bus rule, the deploy checklist, the metric definitions, a paragraph about the old Terraform layout nobody has touched since March.

That file is loaded at session start whether the task needs it or not — about 1,200 tokens before the agent has read a single line of code. And the cost is not only the budget: instructions compete for attention, so 340 lines of everything means nothing stands out. The agent obeys the parts it happens to weight.
steps.youDo: Count your own: wc -l CLAUDE.md. If you scroll past irrelevant sections when you edit it, the agent is reading those sections in full, every session.

steps.title: Split it along the lookup path
narrative: The mechanism the pattern rides on is simple and worth stating exactly: the agent loads CLAUDE.md files from your current working directory up to the repository root. Start it inside services/billing/ and it loads that file plus every parent's — and nothing from sibling directories.

So the split writes itself. Repo-wide facts stay at the root and stay short: what the services are, where shared code lives, how commits are named, which directories are generated. Everything a single service owns moves into that service's own file, where it costs zero tokens in every session that works elsewhere.
steps.youDo: Create labs/sample-project/CLAUDE.md (repo-wide facts only) and labs/sample-project/services/billing/CLAUDE.md (stack specifics). Check: the root file under 25 lines, the billing file mentioning nothing about orders or notifications.

terminal.text: Write  labs/sample-project/CLAUDE.md

# Repository Structure
Three services under services/: billing, orders, notifications.
Shared code in shared/ (auth, db pool, event bus). Tests: `pytest`.

# Commit Conventions
- Prefix commits with the service name: "billing: fix webhook idempotency"
- knowledge/ is refreshed by the post-commit hook — never hand-edit
  generated Dependencies sections
Write  labs/sample-project/services/billing/CLAUDE.md

# Billing Service
FastAPI app in app.py. Domain logic in invoice.py, webhooks in webhooks.py.
## Code Patterns
- Every route verifies auth via shared.auth.verify_token — never inline JWT
- State changes publish via shared.events.publish; consumers stay isolated
- Raise WebhookError for bad payloads; app.py maps it to HTTP 400

steps.title: What the agent does differently
narrative: Start the agent from services/billing/ and ask something that spans both files. It answers the commit convention from the root file and the WebhookError → HTTP 400 mapping from the service file — without opening a single source file, because both facts were already in context before the question arrived.

The second difference is where it goes when the answer isn't pre-loaded. Told that every route verifies auth via shared.auth.verify_token, it opens that path first instead of fanning out through the repo looking for something auth-shaped. The originating case study for this pattern reports 147 file reads dropping to about 12 on that split alone, and 340 startup lines dropping to roughly 90.
Hold that reported number loosely — it is someone else's before/after, on someone else's repo. The next two steps are ours.

view.text: A single reported session, on a repo we cannot inspect, with all six patterns applied at once — so it cannot tell you what the layered files alone are worth. We ran that experiment separately, on two repos, with three fresh sessions per cell. It is less flattering.

steps.title: Measured: 22 CLAUDE.mds on spring-framework
narrative: The init arm of Capstone 2 is this pattern and nothing else: a generated CLAUDE.md in every spring-* module — 22 files across 9,195 Java files — with the same tools, same questions and same model as the baseline. The only variable is the repo state. Every figure below is a median of three independent fresh sessions.

The headline is a wash: 600K vs 585K all-in, +2%. But the average hides the actual finding. On S1 the map sent the agent straight to the right module and won 30% in two turns instead of three. On S2 the auto-loaded context never paid for itself and cost +58%. Structural questions overall got worse by 16%; logic questions got 7% better.
And it is not free to create. Generating those 22 files ran ~$0.15 and ~35 seconds per module, about $3.40 once — which amortizes only across sessions that land on the winning pattern.

steps.title: 36 files, and a single root file is the best arm
narrative: Run the same four scenarios on a small repo and the verdict flips. On priorauth-api-boot3 — 36 Java files, a Spring Boot 3 prior-authorization API — the init arm is a single 55-line root CLAUDE.md (for a single-module app you init the root, not each package), and it is the best arm overall: 565K vs 629K, −10%.

The biggest win is on the orientation-heavy logic question — when does MANUAL_REVIEW happen — where 196K over 7 turns became 120K over 3, a −38% swing. The pure-lookup question barely moved: 74K → 77K. And it still loses somewhere: the eligibility-exception question went 199K → 250K.

Two repos, opposite verdicts, same pattern. Which lever wins is a property of the repo and the question mix, not of the tool — which is the same conclusion the ~500-file payoff floor delivered for graphs in M04.

steps.title: Orientation, not an index
narrative: The two grids explain each other once you stop treating CLAUDE.md as a lookup table. It is orientation and conventions context. It pays off when a session's first problem is where do I even start? — the S1 win, the MANUAL_REVIEW win — and it is pure overhead when the agent already knows where to look, which is why the pure-lookup questions moved by single digits or went backwards.

So the placement rule is doing real work, not tidiness. Facts the agent needs every session belong in CLAUDE.md. Procedures and reference material become skills, which cost zero tokens in sessions that do not match their description. Anything canonical — a metric definition, an SLA — belongs in the OKF bundle where a freshness gate can watch it, not duplicated into an instruction file where it will quietly rot.

And keep the scale in view. The layered pattern is the whole of this course's discipline done by hand: a manual index.md hierarchy, a hand-written .graphifyignore, progressive disclosure without any tooling. On a repo small enough that everything fits, the manual version can beat the machinery outright — as 36 files just did.
steps.youDo: Before writing per-module files across a large repo, run the cheap version of our experiment: one root file, three fresh sessions, your own questions. Expand only if the numbers move.

view.text: Per-module CLAUDE.md files on a 9,195-file repo: +16% on structural questions, −7% on logic, +2% overall, plus ~$3.40 to generate. One root file on a 36-file repo: −10%, the best arm in the grid. Neither number licenses "always add CLAUDE.md files". Both license the habit underneath it: write down orientation, measure whether it helped, and delete it if it did not.
